question: A 55-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presents to his primary care clinic. He admits he did not adhere to a low salt diet on a recent vacation. He now has progressive leg swelling and needs two pillows to sleep because he gets short of breath when lying flat. Current medications include aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and furosemide. His physician decides to increase the dosage and frequency of the patient’s furosemide. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is associated with loop diuretics?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) -> inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle -> increase urinary excretion of sodium, chloride, potassium, and water -> lead to electrolyte abnormalities. CHAIN: Loop diuretics -> can cause hypokalemia due to increased potassium excretion -> leads to increased risk of arrhythmias and muscle weakness -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Loop diuretics -> can cause hypomagnesemia due to increased magnesium excretion -> may result in muscle cramps and cardiac arrhythmias -> 75% confidence. CHAIN: Loop diuretics -> can cause hypocalcemia due to increased calcium excretion -> may lead to muscle spasms and tetany -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Loop diuretics -> can cause hyperchloremia due to increased chloride excretion -> may result in metabolic acidosis -> 60% confidence. CHAIN: Loop diuretics -> can cause hypouricemia due to increased uric acid excretion -> may benefit patients with gout but increase the risk of kidney stones -> 80%
analysis: Loop diuretics such as furosemide can lead to electrolyte abnormalities, particularly hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. However, among the given options, hyperchloremia is the electrolyte abnormality associated with loop diuretics.
